Civil servants: under 3% on strike in central government and 146,000 marchers according to the Interior Ministry, 500,000 according to the CGT, as the government holds firm on the index point

On Tuesday, November 17, the civil servants' strike drew fewer people than on November 5: 146,000 marchers across France according to the Interior Ministry, more than 500,000 according to the CGT, and under 3% of staff on strike in the central civil service. The government still refuses to unfreeze the index point [1][2][3].

According to the Interior Ministry, 146,000 people marched across France, including 28,000 in Paris according to the police prefecture. The CGT claims more than 500,000 marchers, including 175,000 in the capital [1][2].
That is far fewer than on Thursday, November 5, when the ministry counted 575,000 marchers and the CGT 1.6 million [2].
As for strikers, the first official figures show about 2.6% of central government staff, compared with nearly 10% on November 5, 3.9% in public hospitals and 2% in local authorities [1][3][4].

The eight civil service unions, including the CFDT, are calling for a rise in the index point, the value used to calculate the pay of all public employees, and for it to be indexed to inflation; the CGT is asking for at least 10% [5][6].

In the National Assembly, David Amiel, Minister for Public Action and Accounts, defended the choice to target the lowest wages: "Raising the index point benefits senior civil servants more than the lowest-paid civil servants" [3].

The government has announced extra index points for 1.35 million of the lowest-paid public employees, worth an average of 350 euros gross over the year, and a 1.6% rise in the minimum wage (Smic) on December 1, for "a little over a billion euros" [7][5].
In the march, Sophie Binet, general secretary of the CGT, warned: "Only meeting our demands will stop our mobilization" [6].
Key takeaway: the mobilization is fading, but the union front remains united and the dispute is not settled, a few weeks before workplace elections in the civil service [2][8].

The government is betting on targeting. A general rise in the index point would benefit all public employees, including the best paid, and would cost more, while Paris has set itself a public deficit target of 5% of GDP in 2027. David Amiel's office says the announced measures do not jeopardize that goal [3].

For the unions, these targeted raises are "crumbs" that "do not address the emergency": with the index point frozen, employees who are not at the bottom of the scale see their pay lose ground to prices [5][3].

What happens next will play out in December. No new strike day has been set, but the CGT's strike notice covers the central civil service until December 31, and Sébastien Lecornu is due to meet the unions again on December 11 [8][3].

If you are a civil servant at the bottom of the pay scale, you should see your payslip rise a little in 2027; otherwise, your pay stays frozen for now. For everyone, the drop in mobilization means fewer closed schools and disrupted transport, but the threat of more strikes before Christmas has not gone away.

news.2026-11-18-xi-apec-shenzhen.title: China: opening APEC in Shenzhen, Xi Jinping denounces "rampant" protectionism and promises a "huge open market", while Beijing threatens Washington with retaliation over chips
news.2026-11-18-xi-apec-shenzhen.summary: On Wednesday, November 18 in Shenzhen, Xi Jinping opened the APEC CEO summit with a call for "free and open" trade. He denounced unilateralism and protectionism on the eve of his summit with Trump and Putin. At the same time, Beijing is promising to hit back at new US restrictions on AI chips [1][2][6].
Xi Jinping spoke on Wednesday morning at the Qianhai International Conference Center in Shenzhen, at the opening of the APEC CEO Summit, held by the forum that brings together Asia-Pacific economies. His speech was titled "Keeping confidence and moving forward with courage for a bright future in the Asia-Pacific" [3].

He said global growth "lacks momentum" and that "unilateralism and protectionism" are "rampant" [2][3]. He called for "free and open" trade, without barriers to investment, with the World Trade Organization (WTO) at its center [1].
The Chinese president promised that his country would offer companies from around the world a "very large open market" and would increase its imports of quality goods and services [5].

He presented China's next five-year plan (2026-2030) as an invitation to foreign companies, backed the creation of an alliance of the world's economic "bay areas" and revived the idea of a Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific [4][7].

The day before, Tuesday, November 17, China's Commerce Ministry said it was "firmly opposed" to a new US rule that further restricts China's access to the most advanced AI chips, such as Nvidia's, and promised "countermeasures" if Washington persists [6].
Published on November 16, the rule requires a license for AI chips bound for data centers serving Chinese groups, including some shipments to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil [8].
news.2026-11-18-xi-apec-shenzhen.why.0: Key takeaway: Xi Jinping is casting himself as a champion of free trade against Trump's America, just before hosting the US president and Vladimir Putin [1][2].
news.2026-11-18-xi-apec-shenzhen.why.1: The message is aimed at business leaders worldwide, in a city that symbolizes China's tech success. But Washington, Brussels and other capitals worry about China's dominance of supply chains, which gives it geopolitical leverage. Beijing replies that its model suits an economy that is still catching up with the richest countries [1].
news.2026-11-18-xi-apec-shenzhen.why.2: The chip issue complicates the meeting. The new US restrictions could weaken the trade truce between the two countries, Reuters notes [1]. Chinese diplomats are nonetheless promising a three-way summit of "historic significance" on Thursday, November 19 in Shenzhen [9].
news.2026-11-18-xi-apec-shenzhen.why.3: The summit is also due to publish a "Shenzhen Initiative", the first time APEC business leaders have adopted their final text in this form [3].
news.2026-11-18-xi-apec-shenzhen.forMe: What is at stake in Shenzhen affects your daily life: China makes a large share of your electronic devices, and the battle over AI chips weighs on the tech giants that feature heavily in savings funds. A new escalation between Beijing and Washington could make some products more expensive.

United States: Microsoft, air traffic control, JPMorgan, NSA... a string of outages in six days, and even Republicans are demanding answers

In less than a week, the United States has suffered one IT outage after another: Microsoft's email service, air traffic control, JPMorgan Chase bank, United Airlines, then a classified NSA network on Tuesday, November 17. The companies and the White House say there is no evidence of a cyberattack, but lawmakers from both parties are demanding answers [1][2][3].
From November 11 to 14, a global Microsoft outage prevented users from accessing Outlook and other software. Microsoft blames a bug and overloaded servers [1][3].
On November 13, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) had to halt takeoffs nationwide, a rare event. It blames a faulty router, a device that directs data across its network [1].

On Monday, November 16, JPMorgan Chase, the country's largest bank, experienced delays in its services. It blames a software bug in its own hardware and denies any cyberattack [1]. The same day, United Airlines delayed more than 100 flights because of a system that calculates aircraft weight at departure [1][5].

On Tuesday, November 17, a key classified network of the NSA, the US electronic intelligence agency, went down for several hours. The agency says its essential capabilities remained operational and that the outage does not appear to have been caused by a cyberattack [1][3].

Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader in the House of Representatives, is calling for classified briefings for the "Gang of Eight" (the leaders of Congress and of the intelligence committees), then for rank-and-file lawmakers from both parties [2].

Republican James Lankford, senator from Oklahoma, warns: "We can't assume it's a random bug when there are so many things in a row". His colleague Josh Hawley speaks of "the greatest coincidence in the history of the world" if it is all chance [3].
The White House says it has no evidence of a link between these outages or of a coordinated attack. Donald Trump reportedly summed it up as: "It's fine" [2].

Key takeaway: most official explanations point to separate technical failures, not an attack. But their pile-up within a few days, across banking, aviation, tech and intelligence, is fueling doubt even within Trump's camp [1][3].

The former head of the US cybersecurity agency (CISA), Chris Krebs, believes these incidents appear unrelated [3]. According to researchers interviewed by NBC News, computer systems are fragile and prone to failure, and artificial intelligence does not help [1].

The issue is becoming political. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blames aging equipment and a Congress that has not funded its replacement [2]. Jeffries, who spoke with him, says he has "more questions than answers" about what happened and why [2].

Republican Mike Lawler, a New York congressman, is also asking for an "immediate" briefing: "Some of this may be a coincidence, but we need to take cybersecurity and the malicious use of AI seriously" [3][4].

For you, it is a concrete reminder: your bank, your flight or your email depend on a few big IT systems, often American. An outage at Microsoft also hits French companies that use Outlook. Keep a backup means of payment [1].

Egypt: before the World Economic Forum meeting in Cairo, Sisi promises a 2027-2030 plan in December and assures investors they are "safe"

On Tuesday, November 17 in Cairo, President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi urged the major global companies gathered by the World Economic Forum to invest more in Egypt. He touted a 25.9% rise in private investment and announced a 2027-2030 economic program for December [1][2].
The World Economic Forum, the organizer of the Davos meeting, held a "country strategy dialogue" in Cairo with the Egyptian government, bringing together business leaders and public officials [6][4].
Sisi said private investment had grown by 25.9% in the first quarter of the 2025-2026 fiscal year and now accounted for 66% of total investment [2][5].
He cited reforms made for businesses: customs clearance of goods cut to about two days and new laws to make it easier to repatriate profits abroad [2].
He said all amounts owed to foreign oil and gas partners had been paid as of June 30, 2026 [2].

The 2027-2030 program, to be presented in December, aims to boost productivity and the role of the private sector. Targets cited: industry at 20% of output by 2030 and 45% renewable electricity by 2028 [1].
The government is also targeting 5.4% growth and 79 billion dollars of investment for the 2026-2027 fiscal year, according to a plan presented to Sisi on November 15 [3].
The day before, November 16, a second China-Egypt investment forum brought together about 300 companies and institutions from both countries in Cairo [7].
Key takeaway: Egypt is trying to attract private money to take over from the state. Sisi highlighted 5.1% growth and the upcoming end of its program with the IMF [1][2].

The message is aimed at wary investors. Paying arrears to oil companies and making it easier to take profits out addresses their two big fears: not getting paid and not being able to get their money back [2]. Sisi put it this way: any investor can be sure their investments will be "safe" [5].

The limits remain visible. The IMF found that sales of state-owned companies were moving more slowly than planned [1]. And Sisi acknowledged that tensions around Iran and the Strait of Hormuz had clouded the outlook for the country's logistics zones [2].
Egypt also wants to bet on new sectors: data centers, green hydrogen and a second national strategy for artificial intelligence [2].

Egypt is a very popular holiday destination and a key transit country for trade between Europe and Asia. A more stable economy means less risk of a sudden currency crisis and abrupt price rises on the ground. But the tensions around Hormuz are a reminder that the whole Middle East remains fragile [2].

news.2026-11-18-angola-banque-centrale-b: Angola: with inflation at its lowest since 2015, the central bank cuts its rate for the fourth time in a row, to 14%

On Tuesday, November 17, the National Bank of Angola cut its policy rate by 0.75 points, from 14.75% to 14%. It is its fourth consecutive cut. It is relying on inflation that fell to 8.16% year on year in October, its lowest level since March 2015 [1][2].
The monetary policy committee of the National Bank of Angola (BNA) met on November 16 and 17 in Saurimo, in Lunda Sul province, far from the capital Luanda [4].

The policy rate, called the "BNA rate", goes from 14.75% to 14%. Governor Manuel Tiago Dias justified the decision by "the continued slowdown in inflation" and "favorable macroeconomic prospects" [1][2].
The other rates follow: the rate at which the BNA lends to banks overnight falls from 15.75% to 15%, and the rate it pays on their deposits from 13.75% to 13% [3].
It is the fourth cut in a row in 2026, after 0.5 points in May, 1.25 points in July and 1 point in September [1].

According to the national statistics institute (INE), inflation fell to 8.16% year on year in October, from 8.43% in September. Food and non-alcoholic beverages alone account for 5.62 points of it [5].

In September, the BNA raised its growth forecast for 2026 to 6.15%, from 3.6% in July, thanks to oil as well as the rest of the economy, and was targeting year-end inflation of 8.6%, give or take one point [6][7].
Key takeaway: Angola, a major oil producer long plagued by high inflation, has calmed price rises enough to make credit cheaper, a signal for businesses and households [1][5].

A policy rate is the price at which the central bank lends to banks. When it falls, banks can offer cheaper loans, which helps investment. With a rate of 14% and inflation at 8.16%, the rate remains about 6 points above price growth: the BNA is keeping a safety margin [1][5].

The country is benefiting from high energy prices linked to the war with Iran, as it exports a lot of crude [6]. But Liandra da Silva, an economist at Nedbank, warned in September that rising shipping costs and import prices could still reignite inflation [6][7].
The weight of food in inflation also shows the country's fragility: a bad harvest or a rise in import prices can quickly reverse the trend [5].

For you, the direct effect is small: Angola plays little part in what you buy. But an oil-producing country that stabilizes its prices and sees growth pick up becomes more attractive to foreign companies, European ones included [6][7]. It is also a good example of how a central bank cuts rates step by step as inflation falls, without letting go all at once [1].

Salesforce falls more than 9%, its worst session since 2024: software giants pay the price of AI fears on the eve of Anthropic's IPO

On Tuesday, November 17, Salesforce lost more than 9% on Wall Street, its biggest one-day drop since May 2024, dragging down ServiceNow, Intuit and Workday. Investors fear that AI agents will cut into their revenue, and some funds are selling ahead of Anthropic's giant IPO, expected on Thursday [1][2][5].

Salesforce, the customer relationship management software giant, fell about 9% on Tuesday (9.4% according to GuruFocus), to about 194 dollars; according to Barron's, cited by MLQ.ai, it was the worst performer in the S&P 500 that day [4][14][15].
ServiceNow, Atlassian and Workday fell 5.8% to 6.5%; the US software index fund (IGV) lost more than 3% [3][4]. Intuit, the maker of accounting and tax software, also fell sharply [1].
Investors fear that AI agents, programs that carry out tasks on their own, will reduce the number of per-user licenses, the basis of these software makers' revenue [1].
Rishi Jaluria, a software analyst at RBC Capital Markets, summed up the fear: "AI companies are going to try to destroy Salesforce entirely" [1].

In the background: Anthropic, the creator of the Claude assistant, is due on Wednesday, November 18 to price 825 million shares at between 70 and 78 dollars, to raise up to 64 billion dollars, before its debut on Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT [5]. According to Bloomberg, the company is aiming for the top of the range, or even above [6].
Traders point to funds selling software stocks to free up cash ahead of the deal, without hard evidence of a direct link [1][4]. Salesforce is itself a shareholder in Anthropic [4].
The drop came in a falling market: the S&P 500 lost 1.03% and the Dow Jones 1.64% [7].

Key takeaway: the market is betting that AI could threaten the model of the big software makers, which sell per-user subscriptions. If one agent does the work of several employees, fewer licenses are needed [1].

This is not the first warning of 2026. In February, Anthropic tools able to automate tasks done by lawyers, finance staff or salespeople had already triggered a wave of selling nicknamed the "SaaSpocalypse" [10][11]. In April, ServiceNow plunged despite good results [12][13].
Anthropic's IPO, one of the biggest in history, is also drawing money: to buy the new shares, some fund managers are trimming other tech stocks [1][5].
Next test: Salesforce will report its results on December 2. They will show whether its customers are really cutting their licenses [1].

These names may not mean much to you, but their software runs in many French companies, and they carry a lot of weight in the tech funds and US indices in your life insurance or PEA savings plan. On the work side, the question raised by the markets is yours too: which office tasks will AI take over?

How it works: the "per-seat" model threatened by AI agents

Salesforce, ServiceNow and Workday mainly sell subscriptions: the client company pays every month for each employee who uses the software, known as a "seat" or license. The more equipped employees the client has, the more the software maker earns. An AI agent can carry out repetitive tasks on its own (answering customers, entering data, preparing a file). If clients need fewer people in front of the screen, they buy fewer licenses, and the software maker's revenue falls [1]. Software makers are trying to respond by charging for their own agents, but investors doubt this will make up the difference [1].
Precedents: when software disappoints or scares
Salesforce misses revenue expectations and gives disappointing guidance: the stock plunges about 20%, one of the worst sessions in its history [8][9].
This is the benchmark that Tuesday's drop surpasses: the market harshly punishes the slightest sign of a slowdown [8].
February 2026

After the launch of Claude Cowork in January, then of 11 industry modules on January 30, a wave of selling hits software stocks in early February; a Jefferies analyst nicknames it the "SaaSpocalypse" [11]. The Anadolu agency describes AI advances shaking the whole sector [10].
A simple AI product announcement can wipe hundreds of billions off software makers in a few days [10][11].

ServiceNow beats expectations, but its stock loses about 18% in the session, IBM more than 9%, and the software fund about 6% to 7% [12][13].
When fear of AI dominates, even good results do not reassure [13].

The dollar hits a 19-month high and the euro drops below 1.10: markets take a US rate hike in December for granted

On Tuesday, November 17, the dollar index climbed to 103.66, its highest since April 2, 2025, after five sessions of gains. The euro fell to 1.0985 dollars, its lowest in 19 months. The cause: higher-than-expected US inflation, which is pushing markets to bet on a Fed rate hike in December [1][3].
The dollar index reached 103.66 on Tuesday, a level not seen since April 2, 2025, the day Donald Trump announced his tariffs [1].
The euro slipped to as low as 1.0985 dollars, its lowest in 19 months. The Australian dollar fell to 0.6725 US dollars, its lowest since January, and the New Zealand dollar also dropped [1][2].
According to the CME FedWatch tool, traders now see a rate hike by the Federal Reserve (the Fed, the US central bank) in December as a certainty, with about a 4% chance of a half-point hike [1].

The trigger: in October, US consumer prices rose 0.4% in one month, compared with about 0.3% expected. The Fed had already raised its rates in September, before holding them between 3.75% and 4% in October [5].

The market expects about 0.9 points of US rate hikes over a year, compared with about 0.7 points for the European Central Bank (ECB). For Danske Bank, the euro is falling mainly because of the Fed's hawkish stance [3].

The heavy selling of AI stocks also weighed on currencies seen as risky, such as the Australian dollar [1]. On Tuesday evening, the euro moved back toward 1.10 dollars, after a decline in US industrial production [4].
Key takeaway: on the currency market, the winning currency is often the one whose central bank pays the most; and markets see the Fed raising rates faster and for longer than the ECB [1][3].

The ECB is also expected to raise its rates in December: 64 of the 73 economists polled by Reuters in October expected it, with eurozone inflation close to double the 2% target [6]. Another Reuters poll, of 71 economists, sees the deposit rate rising to 2.75% in December, perhaps for the last time [7].

This return of a strong dollar contrasts with spring 2025: after Trump's tariff announcement, the greenback plunged and the euro rose as high as 1.1144 dollars on April 3, 2025 [9], its highest in five months [8]. Carol Kong, an economist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia, sees the dollar supported by capital drawn in by AI, but cites an "erratic" US policy as a risk [1].

A weaker euro means a more expensive trip to the United States, and goods paid for in dollars, such as oil, cost a little more in euros. On the other hand, French companies that sell in dollars, from luxury goods to aerospace, take in more euros. And if the ECB raises its rates in December, mortgages are likely to stay expensive.

How it works: why a rate hike makes a currency rise

Big investors move their money to where it earns the most, for the same level of risk. If the Fed raises its rates, dollar investments (accounts, US government bonds) earn more. To buy them, you first have to buy dollars: demand for the greenback rises and its price goes up against other currencies. What matters is the gap with other central banks. Today, markets expect about 0.9 points of hikes in the United States over a year, compared with 0.7 points for the ECB [3]: the gap favors the dollar. Markets do not wait for the decision: they move as soon as they change their bets, which is why an inflation figure above expectations is enough to push the dollar up [5].
Precedents: when the dollar crushes the euro
September 22, 2000
The euro, launched the previous year, has just fallen to a record low of 84.37 US cents. The ECB then intervenes alongside the Fed and the Bank of Japan to support it [12][13].
That same day, the euro jumps more than 4%, to 90.30 cents: concerted action by central banks can turn a market around, at least in the moment [13].
The euro falls to 1 dollar, for the first time since 2002 [10], as the Fed raises its rates sharply and Europe fears recession amid soaring energy prices [11].
Same mix as today: a Fed tougher than the ECB and a Europe hit by high energy prices push the euro down [11][6].
April 3, 2025
The day after Trump's tariff announcement, the dollar plunges: the euro rises as high as 1.1144 dollars [9], its highest in five months [8].
The dollar is not always a safe haven: a US policy seen as unpredictable can make it fall, a risk economists still cite today [1][9].

news.2026-11-18-coree-du-sud-kdi-croissa: South Korea: driven by AI chips, expected growth for 2027 rises from 2.2% to 3.9%, according to the state-run KDI

On Wednesday, November 18, the Korea Development Institute (KDI), a state-funded think tank, nearly doubled its growth forecast for 2027: 3.9%, up from 2.2% in August. It also raised its 2026 forecast to 3.8%, from 3.2% [1][2].
The reason: global demand for chips for artificial intelligence, which is boosting exports and factory investment [1][2].
Exports are expected to grow 8.1% in 2027, after 10.3% in 2026 [1].
The KDI is far more optimistic than the IMF, which forecast 3.3% for 2027 on Tuesday, and than the central bank (2.9% in August) [3].
The central bank will update its own figures on November 26 [3].
Key takeaway: South Korea, home of Samsung and SK Hynix, is benefiting fully from the global AI race. Yet the KDI warns that this growing dependence on semiconductors is a risk [1][2].
In other words, if the AI race slows, Korea would be on the front line. The central bank's figure on November 26 will show whether it shares the KDI's optimism [3].
Korean chips power your smartphone, your computer and the servers that run AI. The health of this sector affects the price and availability of these devices.
